title: Verify organizer, instructor, mentor and learner permissions
description: Build a role-to-action matrix for organizer, instructor, mentor and learner workflows using a designated test or staging workspace. Verify each permission in the interface with synthetic accounts, document expected versus observed access and evidence, then prioritize ambiguities or gaps for the product team. Do not change production permissions or use real learner data.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Grade every verified permission gap by severity and say what to do: a triage layer on top of the role-to-action matrix
acceptedWorkstreams.description: The accepted workstream produces the expected-vs-observed permission matrix; this idea adds the layer that turns findings into fixes. Approach: for every verified gap or surprise in the matrix, record a severity grade (for example: 'other learners can open a shared file they should not see' is a data-exposure issue; 'mentor sees a settings tab that does nothing' is UI noise), the affected roles and journeys, and a recommended response (fix, confirm-as-intended, or document). Deliver the matrix with the severity column attached, plus a short disclosure-note format the team can paste into an internal ticket or release note, stating what was verified and with which synthetic accounts. Done when: every expected-vs-observed difference in the matrix has a severity grade and one recommended response, and no finding is left as a bare 'unexpected'. Measured: count of gaps by severity; count with a documented response. Why this fits: the goal asks for evidence of permissions, but evidence without severity cannot be prioritized; this makes each finding actionable without re-testing anything the existing workstream already covers.

upvotes.reason: "Grade every verified permission gap by severity and say what to do: a triage layer on top of the role-to-action matrix" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it fills a gap the goal has open rather than restating what is already covered.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Read the roles from a test workspace and the code, then test each permission with a seeded account per role
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Roles in Zedu aren't fixed in the front end: the Roles & Permissions page (settings/organisation/roles-permissions in Cybertron-HNG/zedu-fe, cybertron-integration) loads them from the API, so the real list has to come from a workspace, not from guesses. Plan: 1) in a test workspace, export the role list and each role's permission toggles, and map organiser, instructor, mentor and learner to the roles that exist (or note there's no role for one of them); 2) seed one account per role and run a fixed checklist: create and archive a channel, post an announcement, pin, upload and delete a file, start a Buzz call, invite people, see member emails; 3) report a matrix of expected against actual for each role, with a screenshot for every failure. Tasks: role inventory and test plan (research), seeded-account test run and matrix (research).

pendingIdeas.title: Check the organiser's audit trail: after a permission change or a deletion, what can anyone prove happened
pendingIdeas.description: The role matrix says who may act. It does not say what record remains when they do. Work: perform the sensitive actions as an organiser (remove a member, change a role, delete a channel, delete a file) and then look for the record: who did it, when, to what, and whether the affected person can see it. Deliver the action-to-record table, the gaps, and the minimum fields an institution would ask for during a dispute, tested against the current workspace rather than described as a wish.

upvotes.reason: A role matrix says who may act, not what record survives; checking the audit trail after a permission change or deletion tests accountability.
A role matrix says who may act, not what record remains. Testing the audit trail after a removal or deletion is what makes oversight answerable.

pendingIdeas.title: Document what a mentor can see of a learner's private messages and files, because oversight and privacy collide here
pendingIdeas.description: Mentors need to see enough to help and not enough to surveil, and the product should be able to say which it is. Work: with two seeded accounts, determine whether a mentor can read learner DMs, open files shared privately, see who downloaded what, and view channel history from before they joined. Deliver the visibility table, the statement a school could publish about it, and the two settings that would need to exist if the answer should differ by workspace.

pendingIdeas.title: Measure how fast a role change takes effect, because a demoted instructor who keeps access for a day is a gap
pendingIdeas.description: Revocation timing is rarely tested and often wrong: permissions cached in the client, a token that lives until expiry, a session that survives the role edit. Work: change a user from instructor to learner (and remove them entirely) while that user has an active session, then record what they can still do at one minute, ten minutes and after a forced refresh. Deliver the timing table, the mechanism responsible, and the recommendation with its cost, since immediate revocation usually means a token or cache change.

upvotes.reason: A demoted instructor who keeps access for minutes is a real risk; measuring how fast a role change takes effect tests the control, not the button.
A demoted instructor who keeps access until the token expires is a real gap. Testing revocation on an active session is the only way to find it.

pendingIdeas.title: Test the negative path through the API, not just the interface, since hiding a button is not a permission
pendingIdeas.description: A role matrix built by clicking around proves what the interface shows, not what the server allows. Work: with a seeded account per role, call the endpoints behind the restricted screens directly, using the same session the app uses, and record status codes and returned fields for each. Compare to what the interface hides. Deliver the endpoint-by-role table with responses, and a severity note for every case where the UI hides an action the API still performs, because that is the finding a product team must act on first.

upvotes.reason: Clicking around proves what the interface shows; testing the server refusal through the API is the only way to prove the permission is enforced.
Hiding a button is not a permission. Calling the endpoints directly with each role's session is the test that proves the server enforces the matrix.
